newsitem.title: UK: UK sends reconnaissance force to central Africa.
newsitem.headline: UK sends reconnaissance force to central Africa.

text.p: Britain said on Thursday it was dispatching a reconnaissance party to Zaire but cautioned it would not send a larger force until the nature of its mission to help more than a million starving refugees was absolutely clear.
Prime Minister John Major said western governments had a strong moral obligation to help ease the crisis and Britain was ready in principle to join a Canadian-led international force.
But he told parliament that the situation on the ground was complex, the terrain was very tough and there was no clear ceasefire between Tutsi rebels and their Hutu foes.

"So before sending British troops or deciding upon the precise numbers, we need to be absolutely clear about what they are being asked to do in detail and the conditions under which they will operate," Major said at question time.

"We also need to look very carefully at the particular circumstances they will face. A reconnaisance team will be travelling to the region today to do this and I hope we will be able to reach a firm decision as to what troops go before too long."
In a follow-on statement to parliament, Defence Secretary Michael Portillo said he had put units of Britain's rapid deployment force on short notice to fly out to Central Africa.
He said each of the nations expected to contribute troops was planning to send the equivalent of a batallion -- some 500-600 people -- plus support troops.

"I therefore imagine that our commitment might be of a similar order, but the most important determinant... would be to ensure they were sufficiently well equipped and armed and there in sufficient numbers to be able to look after themselves and be able to do a good job in saving human life," Portillo said.
He said the mission of the international force would be limited to about four months and they would then hand it over to African nations.
He said a number of African countries could contribute troops, including South Africa, Tunisia, Kenya and Ethiopia.
Portillo said Britian had no vital interest in Zaire but, as a civilised nation, had a humanitarian obligation to assist.

"We can see people about to die in their thousands, and we are one of the few nations on earth who have the military capability to help at least some of them," he said to broad backing from members of parliament from all parties.

Apart from a 20-strong reconnaissance party that will travel to Central Africa within the next 24 hours, Portillo said a senior British military planner was in New York to develop a joint plan with other western governments.

Hours earlier, heavy fighting erupted around the eastern Zairean town of Goma, underlining the complexity of the task facing the force, which would try to open up aid routes to the refugees caught up in the confict.

The United Nations envoy negotiating a mandate for the force with Rwanda and Zaire, whose army is battling Rwandan-backed Tutsi rebels, said it was unclear how the Canadian-led troops could handle armed Hutus using refugees as a screen.
Most are former soldiers of the Rwanda armed forces who fled with Hutu civilians after losing a civil war following the 1994 massacre of Tutsis in Rwanda.
